title: Pratt parsing in 30 lines
hook: How does a Pratt parser handle operator precedence in 30 lines?

scenes.caption: Classic recursive descent needs one function per precedence level; Pratt uses one loop and a table.
scenes.narration: Recursive descent usually needs a function per precedence level. A Pratt parser replaces them with one function and a table of binding powers.

scenes.caption: Each infix operator has a left and a right binding power; left below right means left-associative.
scenes.narration: Each operator has a left and right binding power. Left below right means left-associative. For right-associative caret, the right power is lower.

scenes.caption: The loop keeps extending the left side while the next operator binds tighter than the caller allows.
scenes.narration: Parse an atom, then loop: peek an operator, stop if its left power is below min_bp, otherwise consume it and recurse with its right power.

elements.text:
fn expr(min_bp):
  lhs = atom()
  loop:
    op = peek()
    (l, r) = bp(op)
    if l < min_bp: break
    next()
    rhs = expr(r)
    lhs = Node(op, lhs, rhs)
  return lhs

scenes.caption: For 1 + 2 * 3, the star's higher power makes the recursive call take 2 * 3 first.
scenes.narration: Trace one plus two times three. The call with min_bp two sees star with power three, so it grabs two times three first.

scenes.caption: The same table gives left- and right-associativity; prefix, postfix and calls extend the atom step.
scenes.narration: For one minus two minus three, the inner call stops at minus, so grouping is left. Caret's lower right power nests rightward.

items: Prefix: parse in atom() with a bp
Postfix and calls: loop like infix

takeaway: A Pratt parser turns precedence into a table of binding powers and a single loop, so adding an operator is one table entry.
